brief: An n x m river grid has depths a[i][j] (banks a[i][1]=a[i][m]=0). A support at (i,j) costs a[i][j]+1; a bridge in a row needs supports at columns 1 and m with at most d empty cells between consecutive supports. Build bridges on k consecutive rows with minimum total cost.
key_idea: Per row, dp[j]=a[j]+1+min(dp[j-d-1..j-1]) using a monotonic deque; then minimum sliding sum of k consecutive row costs.
solution:
1. For each row: dp[1]=1; for j>1, dp[j]=a[j]+1+min dp[t] for t in [j-d-1, j-1] (gap |j-t|-1<=d).
2. Maintain that window minimum with a monotonic deque of indices (pop front if index < j-d-1, pop back while dp[back]>=dp[j]).
3. cost[row]=dp[m]; use long long (up to 2e5*1e6).
4. Answer = min over i of cost[i]+...+cost[i+k-1] (prefix sums or sliding window).
dry_run:
Own example: one row a=[0,5,1,0], d=1, k=1.
dp1=1; dp2=5+1+dp1=7; dp3=1+1+min(dp1,dp2)=3; dp4=0+1+min(dp2,dp3)=4.
Row cost 4 (supports at columns 1,3,4).

brief: n chains (simple paths of c_i vertices) are linked: chain i's first vertex joins vertex a_i of chain i-1 and its last vertex joins vertex b_i of chain i-1. Find the longest simple cycle length.
key_idea: cur = best path length that closes on chain i's left side; either close directly between a_i and b_i or extend the previous open cycle, minus the a-b segment.
solution:
1. Process chains i=2..n; d=|a_i-b_i|.
2. A cycle whose rightmost chain is i uses c_i-1 inner edges + 2 link edges = c_i+1, plus a path on chain i-1.
3. If i==2 or d==0: cur=c_i+1+d (can't extend through equal attach points).
4. Else cur=c_i+1+max(d, cur_prev-d) (go outward around previous cycle instead of directly).
5. ans=max over all cur; use long long.

brief: A tree with colored vertices; choose a root so that every subtree except the whole tree is single-colored. Print YES and such a root, or NO.
key_idea: The root must touch every edge whose endpoints differ in color.
solution:
1. Count bad edges (endpoint colors differ): cnt; for each vertex count bad edges incident: bad[v].
2. If some v has bad[v]==cnt, rooting at v makes every child subtree contain no bad edge -> monochrome. Print YES v.
3. Otherwise any root leaves a bad edge inside some child subtree -> NO.
4. cnt==0: any vertex (e.g., 1) works.
dry_run:
Sample 1: edges 1-2,2-3,3-4, colors 1 2 1 1.
Bad edges: 1-2, 2-3 -> cnt=2.
bad[1]=1, bad[2]=2, bad[3]=1, bad[4]=0 -> vertex 2 -> YES 2.

brief: On an n x n board you place white rooks and the computer mirrors each move (r,c) with a black rook at (c,r) (skipped if r==c); no two rooks share a row/column. Given k moves already made, count distinct final configurations mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Only the number m of free rows/cols matters; dp[m]=dp[m-1]+2(m-1)dp[m-2].
solution:
1. Each given move with r==c uses 1 row/col, otherwise 2; m = n - used.
2. On m free lines, the smallest free index either gets a diagonal rook (dp[m-1]) or is paired with one of the m-1 others in 2 ways (white at (r,c) or (c,r)): 2(m-1)dp[m-2].
3. dp[0]=dp[1]=1; precompute up to 3e5 mod 1e9+7.
4. Print dp[m].

brief: Repeat n times: delete one element of the array, then add the MEX of the remaining array to m. Minimize final m.
key_idea: Lower the MEX in jumps: dp[j]=min over i>j of dp[i]+(cnt[j]-1)*i+j, starting from dp[mex]=0.
solution:
1. Let M = current MEX (<= n); only values < M matter, cnt[v] their counts.
2. Optimal play: pick a value j<M, delete all its copies; while deleting the first cnt[j]-1 copies MEX stays i, last deletion makes MEX j.
3. dp[M]=0; for j from M-1 down to 0: dp[j]=min over i in (j, M] of dp[i]+(cnt[j]-1)*i+j.
4. Once MEX is 0 every later add is 0; answer dp[0]. Use long long.

brief: Fence of n sections of height k; section i's base must be in [h_i, h_i+k-1] (exactly h_1 and h_n at the ends) and neighbors must overlap by at least 1. Decide if possible.
key_idea: Track the interval [lo,hi] of feasible base heights section by section.
solution:
1. lo=hi=h_1.
2. For i=2..n: lo=max(lo-(k-1), h_i), hi=min(hi+(k-1), h_i+k-1) (overlap means |base_i - base_{i-1}| <= k-1).
3. If lo>hi -> NO.
4. At the end require lo<=h_n<=hi (the last section must sit exactly on h_n).
dry_run:
Sample 3: k=2, h=3 0 2.
lo=hi=3.
i=2: lo=max(2,0)=2, hi=min(4,1)=1 -> lo>hi -> NO (matches).
Sample 2: k=3, h=0 2: lo=max(-2,2)=2, hi=min(2,4)=2; h_n=2 in [2,2] -> YES.

brief: Array a with costs c; changing position i costs c_i and sets it to any value. Make the array non-decreasing at minimum total cost.
key_idea: Kept positions must form a non-decreasing subsequence; maximize kept weight -> answer = sum(c) - max-weight non-decreasing subsequence.
solution:
1. Changed positions can always be filled with suitable values, so only kept ones matter.
2. dp[i]=c_i+max(0, max dp[j] over j<i with a_j<=a_i).
3. best=max dp[i]; answer = sum c - best.
4. n<=8000 total, so O(n^2) is fine (or use BIT over compressed values for O(n log n)). Use long long.
dry_run:
Own example: a=[3,1,2], c=[1,5,5].
dp1=1, dp2=5 (a1=3>1), dp3=5+max(dp2)=10 (a2=1<=2; a1=3>2).
sum c=11, best=10 -> answer 1 (change the 3).

brief: Rooted tree (root 1). A chip moves from v to a vertex one level deeper that is not v's child (from the root any depth-1 vertex is allowed). Count all valid visit sequences starting at the root, mod 998244353.
key_idea: dp[v]=1+(sum of dp over next level)-(sum of dp over v's children), processed deepest level first.
solution:
1. Compute depth (p_i<i so one forward pass) and group vertices by depth.
2. dp[v] = number of sequences starting at v = 1 (stop) + sum of dp[u] for allowed next u.
3. For v!=root: allowed = all of depth d+1 minus children of v: dp[v]=1+S[d+1]-childSum[v].
4. For root: dp[1]=1+S[1]. Process depths from deepest up, mod arithmetic.
5. Answer dp[1].

brief: Array where all elements are +-1 except at most one arbitrary x. Output all distinct subarray sums (empty subarray gives 0) in ascending order.
key_idea: With +-1 steps, achievable sums form a contiguous range; split into segments avoiding x (range containing 0) and segments containing x (another range), output their union.
solution:
1. Let k be the index of x (if none, only case A).
2. Case A (segments not containing k): Kadane max and min subarray sum resetting at k; range [mn,mx] (both include 0 via empty).
3. Case B (segments containing k): with prefix sums P, max = max P[r] (r>=k) - min P[l-1] (l<=k); min = min P[r] - max P[l-1]. Range [lo,hi] is contiguous.
4. Output union of the two integer ranges sorted without duplicates (merge if they overlap).
dry_run:
Sample 4: [7,1], x=7 at index 1.
Case A: only segment [1] -> range [0,1].
Case B: P=[0,7,8]; max=8-0=8, min=7-0=7 -> [7,8].
Union: 0 1 7 8 -> count 4 (matches).

brief: Beacons at distinct positions a_i with power b_i; activated right to left, each destroys beacons to its left within distance b_i. You add one beacon to the far right (activated first) with any power. Minimize destroyed beacons.
key_idea: dp[i] = destroyed among first i beacons if beacon i is activated; added beacon destroys a suffix.
solution:
1. Sort by position.
2. For beacon i (1-indexed): j = number of beacons with position < a_i - b_i (lower_bound).
3. dp[i] = dp[j] + (i-1-j) (beacons j+1..i-1 die, beacon j then activates).
4. Added beacon destroys beacons i+1..n: answer = min over i of dp[i]+(n-i).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Binary array; flip at most k zeros to ones to maximize the longest block of consecutive ones. Print the length and one resulting array.
key_idea: Longest window containing at most k zeros; then set every element in that window to 1.
solution:
1. Two pointers l,r with zeros = count of zeros in [l,r].
2. Extend r; while zeros>k move l right (decrement when a[l]==0).
3. Track best length and its left endpoint bl.
4. Set a[bl..bl+best-1]=1 and print. Edge: k=0 still works (longest run of ones; may be 0).
dry_run:
Sample 1: n=7,k=1, a=1 0 0 1 1 0 1.
r=0..2: at r=2 zeros=2 -> l moves to 2.
r=3..6: window [3,6]=1 1 0 1 zeros=1 length 4 (best, l=3).
Set a[5]=1 -> 1 0 0 1 1 1 1, answer 4 (matches).

brief: n goods with prices a_i and p coins; buy one good for its price, or k goods for the price of the most expensive among them. Maximize goods bought.
key_idea: Sort ascending; dp[i]=dp[i-k]+a[i] (bundle ending at i), and for i<k dp[i]=dp[i-1]+a[i].
solution:
1. Sort prices ascending (cheapest goods are always optimal to take).
2. dp[i] = minimal cost to buy the i cheapest goods (1-indexed).
3. i<k: dp[i]=dp[i-1]+a[i] (single purchases as prefix); i>=k: dp[i]=dp[i-k]+a[i] (last k bought as one bundle).
4. Answer = largest i with dp[i]<=p (0 if none). Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: sorted 2 3 4 5 7, k=2, p=6.
dp1=2, dp2=dp0+3=3, dp3=dp1+4=6, dp4=dp2+5=8, dp5=dp3+7=13.
Largest i with dp<=6 is 3 -> 3 (matches).

brief: Count permutations of 1..n with at least n-k fixed points (k<=4).
key_idea: Choose which m<=k positions move and derange them: sum C(n,m)*D(m).
solution:
1. Derangement numbers D(0..4)=1,0,1,2,9 (D(m)=(m-1)(D(m-1)+D(m-2))).
2. For m=0..k add C(n,m)*D(m).
3. C(n,m) computed directly with long long (n<=1000, m<=4 fits).
4. No modulus needed (max about 3.7e11).

brief: n=2^d. Bob picks a in [1,n]; Alice may halve (if even) or subtract 1 and learns the power of 2 dividing the current value after each move. Count a for which Alice cannot reach 0 within k moves.
key_idea: Alice can always play greedy (halve when even, subtract when odd), so cost(a)=bitlen(a)-1+popcount(a); count numbers with cost>k via binomials.
solution:
1. The feedback (v2 of the current value, -1 at 0) tells Alice the parity, so greedy is playable and optimal: cost = (bitlen-1) halvings + popcount subtractions.
2. For bit length L (1..d), top bit fixed, j ones among L-1 lower bits: cost = L+j; add C(L-1,j) whenever L+j>k.
3. a=n=2^d has cost d+1; count it if d+1>k.
4. d<=30, so loops are tiny; if k>=2d+... the answer is just 0 naturally.
dry_run:
Sample n=16 (d=4), k=5.
L=4: cost 4+j>5 -> j>=2: C(3,2)+C(3,3)=4.
L<=3: max cost 3+2=5, none. a=16 cost 5, not counted.
Total 4 (matches).

brief: n x m grid. One person walks top-left to bottom-right (down/right), the other bottom-left to top-right (up/right). They meet in exactly one cell which neither counts. Maximize total collected.
key_idea: Four corner DP tables; meeting cell (i,j) is entered/left in one of two crossing patterns.
solution:
1. d1[i][j]: best from (1,1) to (i,j); d2: from (i,j) to (n,m); d3: from (n,1) to (i,j); d4: from (i,j) to (1,m).
2. For interior cells (1<i<n, 1<j<m) since the meeting cell must be crossed straight:
3. Option A: d1[i][j-1]+d2[i][j+1]+d3[i+1][j]+d4[i-1][j] (A horizontal, B vertical).
4. Option B: d1[i-1][j]+d2[i+1][j]+d3[i][j-1]+d4[i][j+1] (A vertical, B horizontal).
5. Answer max over all; long long safe.
dry_run:
Sample: 3x3 with 100s and center 1. Meet at (2,2).
Option A: d1[2][1]=200, d2[2][3]=200, d3[3][2]=200, d4[1][2]=200.
Total 800 (matches).

brief: String s of R/G/B and integer k; find the minimum changes so that some length-k substring of s is a substring of RGBRGB...
key_idea: Try the 3 phase shifts of RGB; for each, sliding-window count of mismatches over length k.
solution:
1. For shift o in {0,1,2}: mismatch[i] = (s[i] != "RGB"[(i+o)%3]).
2. Sliding sum of mismatch over windows of length k; track the minimum.
3. Answer = min over the three shifts.
4. Total O(3n) per query; sum n bounded.
dry_run:
Sample 1: s=BGGGG, k=2.
Shift 0 pattern RGBRG: mismatch 1,0,1,1,1 -> windows 1,1,2,2.
Other shifts give >=1 too -> answer 1 (matches).

brief: Text t (|t|<=100) and n<=10 strings; one step colors one occurrence of a string in t. Find the minimum number of steps to color all of t (print the steps) or -1.
key_idea: Interval covering: from the first uncovered position, pick the occurrence starting at or before it that reaches furthest right.
solution:
1. Enumerate all occurrences (start p, string w) by brute-force matching: intervals [p, p+|s_w|-1].
2. covered = 0 (first uncovered index). While covered < |t|:
3. Among occurrences with start <= covered, choose the one with maximum end; if max end < covered -> print -1.
4. Record (w+1, p+1), set covered = end+1. Steps count is minimal by the classic greedy exchange argument.
complexity: O(|t| * n * |s| ) to find occurrences, O(|t|^2 * n) greedy
dry_run:
Own example: t=bababa, s1=ba, s2=aba.
Occurrences: ba@0,2,4; aba@1,3.
covered=0: starts<=0 -> ba@0 end 1 -> covered=2.
covered=2: aba@1 end 3, ba@2 end 3, aba@... choose end 3 -> covered=4; then ba@4 end 5 -> done, 3 steps.

brief: n people in a line; person i claims a_i liars to their left. Honest people tell the truth, liars may say anything, and no two liars are adjacent. Count possible honest/liar assignments mod 998244353.
key_idea: dp[i]=#configs of first i with person i honest: from i-1 honest (a_i==a_{i-1}) or i-1 liar and i-2 honest (a_i==a_{i-2}+1).
solution:
1. Add virtual honest person 0 with a_0=0, dp[0]=1.
2. If person i is honest, the liar count left of i is exact; if i-1 is liar then i-2 is honest and liars-left-of-i = a_{i-2}+1.
3. dp[i] = (a_i==a_{i-1} ? dp[i-1] : 0) + (i>=2 && a_i==a_{i-2}+1 ? dp[i-2] : 0).
4. Answer = dp[n] + dp[n-1] (last person honest, or liar with n-1 honest), mod p.

brief: Cut an array of n positive values into m+1 contiguous pieces; m creatures each need a piece with sum >= v, Alice keeps the remaining piece (may be empty). Maximize Alice's piece or print -1.
key_idea: pf[i]=#creatures greedily fed from prefix a[0..i), sf[j]=# from suffix a[j..n); Alice takes a[i..j) with pf[i]+sf[j]>=m.
solution:
1. Greedy from the left: pf[i] = number of pieces with sum>=v cut greedily within the first i elements; similarly sf[j] from the right.
2. If pf[n] < m -> -1.
3. For each i (0..n), find the largest j>=i such that pf[i]+sf[j]>=m (sf is non-increasing in j, so a pointer/binary search works).
4. Alice gets P[j]-P[i]; take maximum. Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) (or O(n) with two pointers), O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 2: a=[1,1,10,1,1,10], m=2, v=2.
pf: [0,0,1,1,1,2,2] (1+1 then 10); sf from right: sf[6]=0,sf[5]=1,sf[4]=1,sf[3]=2,...
i=0: largest j with sf[j]>=2 is 3 -> sum a[0..3)=12.
Answer 12 (matches).

brief: For array a, f(l,r)=sum_{i=l}^{r-1} |a_i-a_{i+1}|*(-1)^(i-l) (formula from the statement image; matches both samples). Find max f over l<r.
key_idea: Build d_i=|a_i-a_{i+1}| with alternating signs; run Kadane twice (starting at even and at odd positions).
solution:
1. d_i=|a_i-a_{i+1}| for i=1..n-1.
2. Sequence b_i = d_i*(-1)^i and c_i = -b_i; a segment starting at even l uses one sign pattern, odd l the other.
3. Kadane on both: max subarray of b starting at even index and of c starting at odd index. Simpler: dp over states (best ending at i with + sign / - sign): pos[i]=max(d_i, neg[i-1]+d_i), neg[i]=pos[i-1]-d_i.
4. Answer = max pos[i] (segment must start with + sign). Use long long.
dry_run:
Sample 1: a=1 4 2 3 1 -> d=3,2,1,2.
pos1=3,neg1=-inf; pos2=max(2,-inf)=2,neg2=3-2=1; pos3=max(1,1+1)=2,neg3=2-1=1; pos4=max(2,1+2)=3.
max pos=3 (matches).

brief: n segments on m cells; segment i exists independently with probability p_i/q_i. Find the probability (mod 998244353) that every cell is covered by exactly one existing segment.
key_idea: Factor out prod(1-p_i); then dp over cells: dp[r]+=dp[l-1]*p_i/(1-p_i) for segments that tile the strip.
solution:
1. Probability of a chosen set T = prod_{i in T} p_i * prod_{i not in T}(1-p_i) = P * prod_{i in T} p_i/(1-p_i), where P=prod (1-p_i).
2. Valid T is exactly a tiling of [1,m] by consecutive segments.
3. Group segments by right end; dp[0]=1; for r=1..m: dp[r]=sum over segments (l,r) of dp[l-1]*w_i, w_i=p_i*inv(q_i-p_i) mod p.
4. Answer = P*dp[m] mod p (p_i<q_i so 1-p_i is nonzero).
complexity: O((n+m) + n log MOD) time, O(n+m) space

brief: Courier goes from (Ax,Ay) to (Bx,By) with Manhattan moves and must visit n houses, all with Ax<x_i<Bx. Minimize total time.
key_idea: Sweep x left to right (horizontal cost Bx-Ax); in each column cover [minY,maxY] ending at bottom or top -> 2-state DP.
solution:
1. Group houses by x; for each distinct x (sorted) keep lo=min y, hi=max y.
2. Horizontal distance is always Bx-Ax (never go back in x).
3. State: (end at lo, end at hi) with best vertical cost; start y=Ay with cost 0.
4. For a column from previous y position py with cost c: endLo=c+|py-hi|+(hi-lo); endHi=c+|py-lo|+(hi-lo); take mins over both previous states.
5. Answer = (Bx-Ax) + min over states of cost+|y-By|. Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: n people, shared box 0 with a_0 decorations and own boxes a_1..a_n. People take turns cyclically in order of permutation p, each taking one decoration from box 0 or their own box, until all are hung. Count permutations where nobody gets stuck, mod 998244353.
key_idea: With S=sum a, position j gets q+1 turns if j<=r else q (q=S/n, r=S%n); person i must have at least a_i turns.
solution:
1. S = a_0+...+a_n total turns; q=S/n, r=S%n; first r positions get q+1 turns, others q.
2. Only the owner can empty his own box, so need turns(i) >= a_i; extra turns use box 0, and box-0 demand sums exactly to a_0, so this is sufficient.
3. If any a_i > q+1 -> 0. Let c = #people with a_i == q+1; they must occupy the first r positions: if c>r -> 0.
4. Answer = r!/(r-c)! * (n-c)! mod p.
dry_run:
Sample 4: n=4, a0=6, a=1 4 2 1 -> S=14, q=3, r=2.
Only a=4 equals q+1 -> c=1 <= r.
Answer = 2!/1! * 3! = 2*6 = 12 (matches).

brief: n stars on a 100x100 grid with initial brightness s (0..c); brightness increases by 1 each moment and wraps from c to 0. Answer q queries: total brightness at time t inside a rectangle.
key_idea: c<=10: keep a 2D prefix count per initial brightness b; brightness at time t is (b+t)%(c+1).
solution:
1. cnt[b][x][y] = number of stars at (x,y) with initial brightness b (stars may share points).
2. Build 2D prefix sums for each b (11 x 101 x 101).
3. Query (t,x1,y1,x2,y2): for each b, k = rectangle count via inclusion-exclusion; add k*((b+t)%(c+1)).
4. Output the sum (fits in int but use long long).

brief: Given a permutation p, count tuples a<b<c<d with p_a<p_c and p_b>p_d.
key_idea: Fix the middle pair (b,c): multiply #a<b with p_a<p_c by #d>c with p_d<p_b, using a 2D prefix-count table.
solution:
1. pre[i][v] = #j<=i with p_j<=v (build row by row: copy previous row, add 1 for v>=p_i). Use short to fit 5001x5001.
2. For each b<c: A=pre[b-1][p_c-1], D=pre[n][p_b-1]-pre[c][p_b-1].
3. Add A*D to the answer (long long).
4. Sum n <= 5000, so O(n^2) table and loop are fine.
dry_run:
Sample 1: p=5 3 6 1 4 2.
(b,c)=(2,3): A=#a<2 with p_a<6 =1; D=#d>3 with p_d<3 = {1,2} =2 -> 2.
(b,c)=(3,5): A=#a<3 with p_a<4 = 1 (p2=3); D=#d>5 with p_d<6 =1 -> 1.
Other pairs give 0; total 3 (matches).

brief: Concatenate 1,2,3,... into one digit string; for each k (up to 1e15) output the sum of the first k digits.
key_idea: Skip whole digit-length blocks, find the last complete number N, use a per-position formula for digit sum of 1..N, then add the leading digits of N+1.
solution:
1. For d=1,2,...: block has 9*10^(d-1) numbers using d*9*10^(d-1) digits; subtract while k exceeds it.
2. Now k digits remain among d-digit numbers starting at 10^(d-1): cnt=k/d full numbers, rem=k%d; N=10^(d-1)-1+cnt.
3. digitSum(1..N): for each place p=10^i: high=N/(10p), cur=(N/p)%10, low=N%p; add high*45*p + cur*(cur-1)/2*p + cur*(low+1).
4. Add the first rem digits of N+1.
5. All in long long (answer ~4.4e15).
dry_run:
Sample k=13: d=1 block uses 9 digits -> k=4, d=2.
cnt=4/2=2 -> N=9+2=11, rem=0.
digitSum(1..11)=45+1+(1+1)=48 (matches).
k=29: k=20 in d=2 -> N=19, rem=0; sum(1..19)=45+10+45=100 (matches).

brief: Count pairs (l,r) with even length r-l+1 such that XOR of the left half equals XOR of the right half.
key_idea: Equal halves <=> XOR of whole segment is 0 <=> px[l-1]==px[r] with l-1 and r of the same parity.
solution:
1. Prefix XOR px[0]=0, px[i]=px[i-1]^a_i.
2. Left xor == right xor iff total xor = 0 iff px[r]==px[l-1]; even length iff r and l-1 have the same parity.
3. Keep cnt[parity][value] (values < 2^20); for i=0..n add cnt[i%2][px[i]] to answer then increment.
4. Answer as long long.
dry_run:
Sample 1: a=1 2 3 4 5, px=0,1,3,0,4,1.
i=3 (odd): px=0, earlier odd indices: 1(px 1) -> 0.
i=5 (odd): px=1, earlier odd with px 1: i=1 -> +1.
Even indices 0,2,4 values 0,3,4 distinct -> total 1 (matches).

brief: n booking requests (group size c_i, payment p_i) and k tables (capacity r_j, one group each). Accept requests and assign tables to maximize total payment; print assignments.
key_idea: Process requests by payment descending; give each the smallest free table that fits.
solution:
1. Sort requests by p descending (ties: smaller c first).
2. Keep free tables in a multiset of (capacity, index).
3. For each request, lower_bound(c); if found, assign it and erase that table.
4. Exchange argument: a higher-paying group never loses by taking the tightest fitting table.
5. Output count, sum, and pairs (any order).
dry_run:
Sample: requests (10,50),(2,100),(5,30); tables 4,6,9.
Sorted: req2 (2,100) -> table 4 (#1); req1 (10,50) -> none; req3 (5,30) -> table 6 (#2).
Output 2 130 with pairs 2 1, 3 2 (matches).

brief: Towns 1..n each get a tower with probability 1/2; find the probability (mod 998244353) that powers can be set so towns 0 and n+1 get no signal and each town 1..n is covered by exactly one tower.
key_idea: Valid tower sets = partitions of 1..n into odd-length blocks, counted by Fibonacci: answer F(n)/2^n.
solution:
1. Each tower covers an odd-length block centered on it; blocks must tile [1..n] exactly.
2. Count of compositions of n into odd parts: dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-3]+... which equals Fibonacci F(n) (F1=F2=1); equivalently dp[i]=sum of dp[i-odd] via prefix sums by parity.
3. Answer = F(n) * inverse(2^n) mod 998244353.
complexity: O(n + log MOD) time, O(1) space
dry_run:

Probability 5/32 (matches the note) -> 842268673 mod p.

brief: Count x in [1,n] with x - digitsum(x) >= s (n, s up to 1e18).
key_idea: f(x)=x-digitsum(x) is non-decreasing, so binary search the smallest x with f(x)>=s.
solution:
1. f(x+1)>=f(x) because adding 1 raises x by 1 and the digit sum by at most 1.
2. Binary search lo=1, hi=n for the smallest x with f(x)>=s.
3. If none (f(n)<s) answer 0, else n-x+1.
4. Note answer x is at most s+9*18+... so search range is small anyway.

brief: n bottle types; type i holds 2^(i-1) liters and costs c_i, unlimited supply. Find the minimum cost to buy at least L liters.
key_idea: Normalize c_i=min(c_i,2*c_{i-1}), then go from the largest bottle down, either filling greedily or overshooting with one extra bottle.
solution:
1. For i>=1: c[i]=min(c[i], 2*c[i-1]) (two smaller bottles may be cheaper).
2. cost=0; for i=n-1..0: k=L/2^i; cost+=k*c[i]; L-=k*2^i; ans=min(ans, cost + (L>0 ? c[i] : 0)).
3. ans=min(ans,cost) at the end (the overshoot option covers buying one extra bottle). Use long long (up to ~1e18).

brief: Split each middle a_i into x_i+y_i=a_i with (x_i-s)(y_i-s)>=0; minimize F=a_1*x_2+y_2*x_3+...+y_{n-1}*a_n.
key_idea: F is linear in each x_i, so only the two extreme valid splits matter; 2-state DP over which extreme is used.
solution:
1. Valid x_i form an interval; extremes: if a_i<=s: lo=0; else lo=min(s,a_i-s); hi=a_i-lo. Options (x,y)=(lo,hi) or (hi,lo).
2. dp[i][0/1] = min F prefix with option 0/1 at i; prevY for i=1 is a_1.
3. dp[i][o] = min over p of dp[i-1][p] + y_{i-1,p} * x_{i,o}.
4. Answer = min over o of dp[n-1][o] + y_{n-1,o}*a_n. Use long long.

brief: Two digit strings a and b; an operation replaces two adjacent digits of either string by their sum mod 10. Maximize the common length after making them equal, or -1.
key_idea: A final string = partition into segments; segments match iff cut points have equal prefix sums mod 10, so it's LCS of prefix-mod sequences.
solution:
1. Pa[i] = (a_1+...+a_i) mod 10, Pb likewise.
2. If Pa[n] != Pb[m] -> -1 (total sum mod 10 is invariant).
3. Choosing cuts i_1<...<i_k=n and j_1<...<j_k=m with Pa[i_t]==Pb[j_t] gives equal strings of length k.
4. Answer = LCS(Pa[1..n-1], Pb[1..m-1]) + 1 (the final pair always matches).
5. O(n*m) LCS with a rolling 1D array (sum of lengths <= 1e4 so at most 25e6 cells).

brief: Rooted tree (root 1) with vertex values a_u and edge weights (possibly negative). Vertex v is sad if some u in its subtree has dist(v,u)>a_u. Remove leaves repeatedly until no vertex is sad; minimize removed leaves.
key_idea: u must be deleted (with its subtree) iff max over ancestors v of dist(v,u) > a_u; that max is a Kadane-style best = max(0, best_parent + w).
solution:
1. DFS from root carrying best = max path sum ending at current vertex from some ancestor: best_u = max(0, best_parent) + w(parent,u) (track max(0,..) for starting fresh).
2. If best_u > a_u, u is sad-causing: cut its whole subtree (don't descend).
3. Count kept vertices; answer = n - kept.
4. Use iterative DFS and long long.
dry_run:
Own example: n=3, a=[5,1,10], edges 1-2 (w=3), 1-3 (w=4).
Vertex 2: best=max(0,0)+3=3 > a_2=1 -> remove subtree {2}.
Vertex 3: best=4 <= 10 -> keep.
Answer = 3-2 = 1. (Sample answer 5 for the 9-vertex input.)

brief: Remove the minimum number of elements so the array cannot be split into two subsequences with equal sums; print removed indices.
key_idea: If a partition exists, remove one element with the smallest power of two in its factorization (an odd element after dividing everything by the common 2^k).
solution:
1. If total sum is odd, or subset-sum dp shows sum/2 is unreachable -> print 0.
2. Otherwise answer is exactly 1: dividing all elements by 2 preserves partitionability, so divide until some element is odd.
3. Removing that odd element makes the remaining total odd -> no equal split.
4. Practically: pick index with minimum lowbit(a_i) (count of trailing zeros).
5. Subset-sum via bitset<200001>.

Trailing zeros: 6->1, 3->0, 9->0, 12->2; first minimum is index 2 (value 3).

brief: n=a!/b!; each round divide n by some x>1 dividing it. For up to 1e6 queries (a,b<=5e6), output the maximum number of rounds.
key_idea: Max rounds = number of prime factors with multiplicity of a!/b! = sum of Omega(k) for k in (b,a].
solution:
1. Always divide by a prime to maximize rounds, so answer = Omega(n).
2. Sieve smallest prime factor up to 5e6; Omega(k)=Omega(k/spf[k])+1.
3. Prefix sums P[k]=sum Omega(1..k) (fits in int? up to ~1.8e7, ok; use long long safe).
4. Answer P[a]-P[b]. Use fast IO for 1e6 queries.
complexity: O(N log log N) precompute, O(1) per query

Total 5 (matches). Sample 1: 3!/1! = 6 -> 2.

brief: Road from 0 to l with n speed-limit signs (position d_i, a_i minutes per km, valid until next sign). Remove at most k signs (not the first) to minimize travel time.
key_idea: dp[i][r] = min time to reach kept sign i having removed r signs so far; transition from previous kept sign p removes the i-p-1 signs between.
solution:
1. Append a virtual sign n+1 at position l.
2. dp[1][0]=0; others INF.
3. For i=2..n+1, for p<i, removed between = i-p-1; for r: dp[i][r+i-p-1] = min(dp[p][r] + a_p*(d_i-d_p)) if r+i-p-1<=k.
4. Answer = min over r<=k of dp[n+1][r].
5. Values up to 1e9 fit in long long.

brief: Given n strings of length m (n,m<=10), find any string s of length m differing from every given string in at most one position, or -1.
key_idea: s differs from a_1 in at most one position, so try a_1 with every single-position change (26*m+1 candidates) and verify.
solution:
1. Candidates: a_1 itself, and a_1 with position j set to each letter.
2. For each candidate, check every a_i: count mismatches <= 1.
3. Print the first candidate that passes; else -1.
4. Cost ~ 26*m * n*m, tiny.

brief: A tree of n cities with directed roads; choosing a capital requires reversing roads so all cities are reachable from it. Output the minimum number of reversals and all optimal capitals.
key_idea: Rerooting: compute reversals for root 1, then moving root across edge u->v changes the count by +1 if the edge points u->v, else -1.
solution:
1. Store each undirected edge with weight 0 if it points away (u->v as given) and 1 if it points toward u.
2. BFS/DFS from 1: cost[1] = sum of weights of edges in direction parent->child (1 means needs reversing).
3. For child v of u via weight w: cost[v] = cost[u] + (w==0 ? 1 : -1).
4. Output min cost and all vertices achieving it in increasing order.

brief: Directed graph with a letter on each node; a path's value is the count of its most frequent letter. Output the maximum path value, or -1 if unbounded (cycle).
key_idea: If there's a cycle the answer is -1; otherwise dp[v][c] = max count of letter c on a path ending at v, in topological order.
solution:
1. Kahn's algorithm; if fewer than n nodes are popped, a cycle exists -> -1 (self-loops count).
2. dp[v][c] initialised with dp[v][s[v]]=1.
3. Processing u in topo order, for each edge u->v and each letter c: dp[v][c]=max(dp[v][c], dp[u][c] + (s[v]==c)).
4. Answer = max over all dp[v][c].

brief: Card w x h and n envelopes; build the longest chain of envelopes strictly increasing in both width and height, with the card fitting strictly inside the first. Print the length and indices (0 if none).
key_idea: Keep only envelopes larger than the card, sort by width then height, and run O(n^2) LIS with strict 2D comparison plus parent pointers.
solution:
1. Filter envelopes with w_i>w and h_i>h; if none print 0.
2. Sort by (w,h).
3. dp[i]=1+max dp[j] over j<i with w_j<w_i and h_j<h_i; store parent.
4. Take the best end, follow parents back, reverse and print original indices.

brief: Array a; one operation sets an element equal to an adjacent element. With at most k<=10 operations, minimize the array sum.
key_idea: Final array = segments each filled with its own minimum; a segment of length len costs len-1 operations.
solution:
1. dp[i][j] = min sum of the first i elements using j operations.
2. Transition: the last segment is a[i-len+1..i] (len <= j+1), all set to its minimum m: dp[i][j] = min dp[i-len][j-len+1] + len*m.
3. Compute m incrementally while extending len backwards.
4. Answer = min over j<=k of dp[n][j]. Use long long.

brief: Spell damage at consecutive seconds can grow by 1 or reset to 1 (costing damage in mana). Monster i at second k_i needs damage >= h_i. Minimize total mana.
key_idea: Each monster needs a ramp starting at k_i-h_i+1; merge overlapping ramps from right to left; a ramp of length L costs L(L+1)/2.
solution:
1. Process monsters from last to first, keeping the current ramp [s,e] (start with s=k_n-h_n+1, e=k_n).
2. If k_i >= s, monster i lies in the ramp: s = min(s, k_i-h_i+1).
3. Else close the ramp: add L(L+1)/2 with L=e-s+1; start a new ramp for monster i.
4. Add the last ramp. Use long long (L up to 1e9).

brief: Values in 1..26, n<=2000. Find the longest subsequence of the form x copies of a, y copies of b, x copies of a.
key_idea: For outer value a and count x, take its x-th occurrence from the left and from the right; the middle is the most frequent value strictly between them (prefix counts).
solution:
1. pre[v][i] = count of value v in a[0..i).
2. Answer starts with max frequency of any value (x=0).
3. For each value a with positions p[0..c-1], for x=1..c/2: l=p[x-1], r=p[c-x]; mid = max over b of pre[b][r]-pre[b][l+1].
4. Candidate 2x+mid; take max.
complexity: O(26 * n * 26 / 2) worst case, O(26 n) space

brief: Array with values 0..63; count non-empty subsequences whose bitwise AND has exactly k set bits, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[v] = number of subsequences (so far) with AND equal to v; only 64 states.
solution:
1. dp[0..63]=0.
2. For each a_i: ndp=dp (skip a_i); for each v: ndp[v & a_i] += dp[v]; ndp[a_i] += 1 (subsequence starting here).
3. dp=ndp, all mod 1e9+7.
4. Answer = sum of dp[v] with popcount(v)==k.

popcount(3)=2 -> answer 1 (matches).

brief: n floors; stairs between i and i+1 cost a_i, elevator costs b_i plus a fixed c per ride. Output the minimum time from floor 1 to every floor.
key_idea: Two states per floor: arrived by stairs, or currently riding the elevator (overhead c already paid).
solution:
1. Going down never helps, so move upward only.
2. s[1]=0 (stairs), e[1]=c (elevator boarded).
3. s[i+1]=min(s[i],e[i])+a_i; e[i+1]=min(s[i]+c, e[i])+b_i.
4. Answer t_i=min(s[i],e[i]).

brief: Compute the sum over all subarrays of XOR(subarray) * length, mod 998244353.
key_idea: Per bit, a subarray (j,r] has the bit set iff prefix bits at j and r differ; keep count and sum of indices of prefixes with each bit value.
solution:
1. Prefix XOR px[0..n].
2. For each bit b (0..29): cnt[2], sum[2] over seen prefix indices j by bit value; start with j=0 (bit 0).
3. For r=1..n: v=bit of px[r]; contributions from j with bit !v: cnt[!v]*r - sum[!v] (sum of lengths r-j).
4. Add that * 2^b to the answer mod p; then record r in cnt[v], sum[v].

brief: Count non-empty subsequences b of a (by index set) where b_i is divisible by i for every position i, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[j] = number of good subsequences of length j; a_i can extend at position d for each divisor d of a_i (d<=n), updated in decreasing d.
solution:
1. dp[0]=1.
2. For each a_i, list its divisors d<=n (trial division up to sqrt).
3. Process divisors in decreasing order: dp[d] += dp[d-1] (decreasing like 0/1 knapsack so a_i is used once).
4. Answer = sum dp[1..n] mod p.

a=1: divisors {1}: dp1=1.
a=2: divisors {2,1}: dp2+=dp1 -> 1; dp1+=dp0 -> 2.
Sum=2+1=3 (matches).

brief: A program of n +/- instructions changes x starting at 0. Each query (l,r) skips instructions l..r; report how many distinct values x takes.
key_idea: Values visited form a contiguous range: combine prefix min/max before l with suffix min/max after r shifted by p[l-1]-p[r].
solution:
1. p[i] = x after i instructions; pmin[i], pmax[i] = min/max of p[0..i].
2. smin[i], smax[i] = min/max of p[j]-p[i] for j in [i..n] (includes 0), computed right to left.
3. Query: base=p[l-1]; lo=min(pmin[l-1], base+smin[r]); hi=max(pmax[l-1], base+smax[r]).
4. Answer hi-lo+1 (steps are +-1 so all values in between are hit).

lo=min(0,-1)=-1, hi=max(0,1)=1 -> 3 (matches).

brief: Pair 2n points on a line into n segments so that any two segments are either nested or of equal length. Count such pairings mod 998244353.
key_idea: dp[n] = (sum of dp[1..n-1]) + d(n): either the outermost segment wraps a smaller good pairing, or all equal-length blocks tile, counted by divisors of n.
solution:
1. Case A: the longest segments are nested outer layers around a good pairing of k<n pairs in the middle; each k in 1..n-1 gives dp[k] ways -> dp[1]+...+dp[n-1].
2. Case B: all segments that are not nested have equal length, forcing a periodic structure: number = number of divisors d(n).
3. Sieve d(1..n) in O(n log n).
4. dp[n] = prefixSum(n-1) + d(n), mod p.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Count arrays of n integers in [0,2^k) where AND of all elements >= XOR of all elements, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Compare bit by bit from the top: per bit count ways AND==XOR (tie) vs AND>XOR (win, then lower bits free).
solution:
1. Per bit, #assignments with an even number of ones = 2^(n-1).
2. n odd: all-ones gives AND=1,XOR=1 (tie); ties per bit = 2^(n-1)+1, AND>XOR impossible -> answer (2^(n-1)+1)^k.
3. n even: tie = 2^(n-1)-1 (even, not all ones), win = 1 (all ones gives AND=1, XOR=0).
4. Answer = tie^k + sum over winning bit i (from top) of tie^(k-1-i) * (2^n)^i, where i = number of lower bits free.
5. Use fast power mod; k=0 -> 1.

Sample 2: n=2 even, k=1: tie=1, win term i=0: 1*1=1 -> 1+1=2 (matches).
Sample 3: k=0 -> 1.

brief: Repeatedly multiply x by one of its own digits; find the minimum number of operations to make x have exactly n digits (n<=19), or -1.
key_idea: BFS over reachable values (only x*2^a*3^b*5^c*7^d, so few states) with a hash set; stop at the first value with n digits.
solution:
1. BFS from x with distance 0; visited set (unordered_set or map).
2. If len(v)==n return dist.
3. Otherwise for each distinct digit d>=2 of v (0 and 1 are useless), push v*d if not visited.
4. Values below 10^18 times 9 fit in unsigned long long.
5. Queue empty -> -1 (e.g., x consisting only of 0/1 digits).
complexity: O(S log S) where S = reachable states (tens of thousands)

Level0: 2; level1: 4; level2: 16; level3: 16*1(no), 16*6=96; level4: 96*9=864, 96*6=576 -> 3 digits.
Answer 4 (matches).

brief: Given n numbers (<=1e7) and m queries [l,r] (r up to 2e9), output the sum over primes p in [l,r] of the count of numbers divisible by p.
key_idea: Sieve to 1e7; f(p)=sum of cnt[multiples of p]; prefix sums over primes; clamp query ranges to 1e7.
solution:
1. cnt[v] = occurrences of value v.
2. Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 1e7; for each prime p, f(p)=sum cnt[p], cnt[2p], ... (computed while crossing out).
3. pre[i] = sum of f(p) for primes p<=i.
4. Query: clamp r=min(r,1e7), l=min(l,1e7+1); answer pre[r]-pre[l-1] (0 if l>r).
5. Use fast IO for n=1e6.
complexity: O(M log log M) precompute (M=1e7), O(1) per query; ~90MB memory

brief: Count index triples i<j<k with a_j=a_i*k and a_k=a_j*k (geometric progression with ratio k).
key_idea: Treat each element as the middle: (#left equal to a/k) * (#right equal to a*k) using two hash maps.
solution:
1. right map = counts of all elements; left map empty.
2. For each j: remove a_j from right.
3. If a_j % k == 0: ans += left[a_j/k] * right[a_j*k].
4. Add a_j to left. Use long long for products and keys (a*k up to 2e14).
5. Works for k=1 and negatives (C++ % with exact division is fine).
complexity: O(n log n) with map (or O(n) with unordered_map)

brief: Array of n values in [0,n]; an operation increments one element. For each i in 0..n output the minimum operations to make MEX exactly i, or -1.
key_idea: Sweep i upward: MEX=i costs (cost to have 0..i-1 present) + cnt[i]; fill each missing value with the largest spare smaller value from a stack.
solution:
1. cnt[v] counts; stack of spare values; base=0; ok=true.
2. For i=0..n: if !ok print -1; else print base+cnt[i] (bump every copy of i up).
3. Then push cnt[i] copies of i onto the stack; if the stack is empty, value i can't be made -> ok=false; else pop top v (largest spare) and base += i-v.
4. Use long long for base.

i=1: print 1; push 1, pop 1.
i=2: print 0; stack empty -> ok=false; i=3: -1.
Output 1 1 0 -1 (matches).

brief: n x m grid of '.'/'#'. Repaint the fewest pixels so that every column is one color and each maximal run of same-colored columns has width between x and y.
key_idea: Column costs to white/black, prefix sums; dp[i][c] = min cost for first i columns ending with a run of color c.
solution:
1. cw[j] = #'#' in column j (cost to make white), cb[j] = n - cw[j]; prefix sums PW, PB.
2. dp[0][0]=dp[0][1]=0; others INF.
3. dp[i][c] = min over len in [x,y], len<=i of dp[i-len][1-c] + cost_c(i-len+1..i); for i-len==0 the previous color doesn't matter (both 0).
4. Answer min(dp[m][0], dp[m][1]).

Runs of width 1 alternate colors: 5 columns * 1 = 5 (matches).

brief: Trees with heights a_i; from tree i the rabbit may jump backward to a taller tree or forward to a shorter tree. For each start, output the maximum reachable height.
key_idea: Boundary between i and i+1 is crossable iff prefix max(1..i) > suffix min(i+1..n); then ans[i]=ans[i+1], else ans[i]=prefix max.
solution:
1. pm[i]=max(a_1..a_i), sm[i]=min(a_i..a_n).
2. From any position in 1..i you can reach pm[i] (jump back to it via chain), and cross to the right part iff pm[i] > sm[i+1].
3. ans[n]=pm[n]; for i=n-1..1: ans[i] = (pm[i] > sm[i+1]) ? ans[i+1] : pm[i].
4. Print ans.

brief: Known die outcomes x_1..x_n. Pick a value a and a range [l,r]; money doubles when x_i==a and halves otherwise, starting at 1. Output a, l, r maximizing the final money.
key_idea: Maximize (#matches - #misses); for each value run Kadane over its occurrence positions, where a gap of g non-matching rounds costs g.
solution:
1. Group indices by value (map value -> positions).
2. For value v with positions p_0<p_1<...: cur score ending at p_j = max(1 (restart at p_j), cur + 1 - (p_j - p_{j-1} - 1)).
3. Track the start index when restarting; update best (score, v, l, r).
4. Segment endpoints are always at occurrences of a, so this covers all optimal answers.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

cur: p1 ->1; p2 -> 2; p4 -> 2+1-1=2; p5 -> 3 (start 1).
Value 3 gives 1. Best: 4 1 5 (matches).

brief: Tree with k marked vertices; f_i = max distance from i to a marked vertex. Output min over i of f_i.
key_idea: Answer = ceil(D/2) where D is the largest distance between two marked vertices (found by two BFS passes).
solution:
1. BFS from any marked vertex; take the farthest marked vertex u.
2. BFS from u; D = max distance to a marked vertex.
3. The middle of that path is within ceil(D/2) of every marked vertex (standard diameter argument), and no vertex can do better.
4. Print (D+1)/2; k=1 gives 0.
dry_run:

brief: n players, each imposter (always lies) or crewmate (always truthful). m comments 'i says j is imposter/crewmate'. Output the maximum number of imposters, or -1 if contradictory.
key_idea: 'imposter' claim means i and j have different roles, 'crewmate' means same roles; 2-color each component with parity edges and take the larger side.
solution:
1. Edge (i,j,w) with w=1 for 'imposter' (different roles), w=0 for 'crewmate' (same).
2. BFS each component assigning color[v]=color[u]^w; a conflict -> -1.
3. Count cnt0, cnt1 in the component; we can flip the whole component, so add max(cnt0,cnt1).
4. Isolated vertices count as imposters (max(1,0)=1).

brief: n players in a circle each attack left (L) or right (R). A player attacked by exactly one neighbor must attack that neighbor back. Find the minimum number of players to switch so that everyone follows this rule.
key_idea: Valid iff no run of 3+ equal letters (circularly); a maximal run of length L needs L/3 changes.
solution:
1. Rotate s so that it starts at a run boundary (s[0]!=s[n-1]).
2. If no boundary exists (all equal): answer (n+2)/3.
3. Otherwise split into maximal runs; add L/3 for each run length L.
4. Changing every third letter of a run breaks it into pieces of length <=2, which is optimal.

Answer 1 (matches). Sample 5: RRRRR -> (5+2)/3=2.

brief: A mouse on a tree starts at st; at step i cheese appears at p_i and the mouse moves one edge toward it (or stays if already there). Output a permutation p of all vertices so the mouse surely ends at en, or -1.
key_idea: Put cheese on vertices in decreasing order of distance from en (en last); the mouse's distance to en ends at 0. Always possible.
solution:
1. BFS from en to get dist[v].
2. Sort vertices by dist descending (bucket by distance); en (dist 0) comes last.
3. Invariant: after processing all vertices at distance >= d, the mouse is within distance d-1 of en... each step toward a vertex at distance d either keeps it within distance <= d or moves it closer.
4. Output the order; -1 never occurs.

brief: Rooted tree, all values start at 0; one operation adds a non-decreasing (root to v) sequence along a root-to-v path. Each vertex must end in [l_v, r_v]. Minimize operations.
key_idea: Bottom-up: a vertex can receive at most the sum of what its children received; if that sum < l_v, spend a new operation and set its value to r_v, else cap at r_v.
solution:
1. Process vertices in decreasing index order (p_i < i ensures children before parents).
2. s[v] = sum of final values passed up from children.
3. If s[v] < l_v: ans++, val[v]=r_v (a new path ending at v, maximal value helps ancestors).
4. Else val[v] = min(s[v], r_v). Add val[v] to s[parent].
5. Use long long sums.

brief: d(n) = sum of divisors of n. For each c (<=1e7) output the smallest n with d(n)=c, or -1.
key_idea: Precompute sigma(n) for all n<=1e7 with a divisor sieve, then ans[sigma(n)] = smallest such n.
solution:
1. sigma[n] for n<=1e7: for each i, add i to all multiples (harmonic sum ~1.6e8 ops) or use a linear sieve.
2. Since sigma(n) >= n+1 > n for n>1, only n<=c matter, so N=1e7 suffices.
3. ans[] init -1; for n from N down to 1: if sigma[n]<=N, ans[sigma[n]]=n (descending keeps the smallest).
4. Answer each query in O(1). Memory ~80MB of ints (limit 512MB).
complexity: O(N log N) precompute, O(1) per query

brief: n trees, some precolored (0 = uncolored); painting tree i with color j costs p[i][j]. Color all uncolored trees so the number of same-color segments is exactly k, minimizing paint; -1 if impossible.
key_idea: dp[i][j][c] = min cost for first i trees with j segments and tree i of color c.
solution:
1. Allowed colors of tree i: only c_i if precolored (cost 0), else all 1..m with cost p[i][c].
2. dp[1][1][c] = cost(1,c).
3. dp[i][j][c] = cost(i,c) + min(dp[i-1][j][c], min over c'!=c of dp[i-1][j-1][c']).
4. Speed up with best and second-best of dp[i-1][j-1][*] (or plain O(n k m^2)=1e8).
5. Answer min_c dp[n][k][c], -1 if INF. Use long long.
complexity: O(n*k*m) time with best-two trick, O(n*k*m) space

brief: Tree with node values; delete between 1 and k-1 edges so that every component has the same XOR. Answer YES/NO.
key_idea: If total XOR X is 0, cutting one edge works; otherwise we need 3 components each with XOR X (k>=3), found by greedy DFS cutting subtrees whose XOR equals X.
solution:
1. X = XOR of all values. If X==0 -> YES (two parts with equal XOR).
2. If k==2 -> NO (two parts would XOR to 0).
3. DFS (post-order) computing subtree XOR; when it equals X, count++ and return 0 to the parent (cut it off).
4. If count >= 2 -> YES (two cut pieces of X plus the rest which is X) else NO.
5. Use iterative DFS for n up to 1e5.

brief: Cities 0..n on a line with directed roads (L/R); after every move all roads flip. For each starting city, output the maximum number of distinct cities visited.
key_idea: Because roads flip every move, a walk in one direction needs an alternating L/R pattern; count alternating run lengths to the left and to the right of each city.
solution:
1. Going left from city i uses road i (s[i-1]) which must be 'L', then road i-1 must be 'R', etc.
2. left[i] = 0 if s[i-1]!='L'; else 1 + (i>=2 && s[i-2]=='R' ? 1 + left[i-2] : 0).
3. right[i] = 0 if s[i]!='R'; else 1 + (i+1<n && s[i+1]=='L' ? 1 + right[i+2] : 0).
4. You can go one way then come back and go the other, so answer = 1 + left[i] + right[i].

brief: Split an array into the minimum number of contiguous segments such that no segment has two elements whose product is a perfect square (k=0, no changes allowed).
key_idea: a*b is a square iff their square-free kernels are equal; greedily cut whenever the current segment already contains the kernel.
solution:
1. Sieve smallest prime factor up to 1e7.
2. kernel(a) = product of primes with odd exponent in a.
3. Scan left to right with a set of kernels in the current segment; if kernel already present, start a new segment (ans++, clear set).
4. Answer = number of segments. Greedy longest segments is optimal.
complexity: O(A log log A + n log a) time

brief: Each friend is an h x w rectangle that may be rotated. For each friend i, output any j whose rectangle fits strictly inside i's (both dimensions smaller, some orientation), or -1.
key_idea: Normalize to (small, big); sort by small; for each group keep the prefix minimum big among strictly smaller small values.
solution:
1. For each friend: s=min(h,w), b=max(h,w). j fits i iff s_j<s_i and b_j<b_i.
2. Sort indices by s.
3. Sweep groups of equal s: answer each member using best (min b, index) over all previous groups; if bestB < b_i answer that index else -1.
4. After the group, update best with the group's members.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Arrays a (hair) and b (target); m razors of sizes x, each usable once on a segment setting a_i=min(a_i,x). Decide if a can become b.
key_idea: Need a_i>=b_i; each position with a_i>b_i needs a razor of size exactly b_i, and one razor of size x covers consecutive needing positions with value x unless a larger b in between blocks it (monotonic stack).
solution:
1. If any a_i<b_i -> NO.
2. Scan i with a stack of active razor values (decreasing from bottom): pop while top < b_i (a larger b blocks smaller razors).
3. If a_i>b_i: if top == b_i reuse that razor; else push b_i and need[b_i]++.
4. Count available razors per size (map); if any need[x] > have[x] -> NO, else YES.

brief: Array a and m queries [l,r]: is the subarray a 'ladder' (non-decreasing then non-increasing)?
key_idea: up[i] = furthest index reachable from i while non-decreasing; down[i] = furthest while non-increasing; answer Yes iff down[up[l]] >= r.
solution:
1. Compute from the right: up[n]=n; up[i] = a[i]<=a[i+1] ? up[i+1] : i.
2. down[n]=n; down[i] = a[i]>=a[i+1] ? down[i+1] : i.
3. Query (l,r): climb to j=up[l] (peak), then descend: Yes iff down[j] >= r.
4. Single-element ranges are always Yes.

Query (5,8): up[5]=6, down[6]=8>=8 -> Yes.

brief: DAG of checkpoints (edges s<t) where checkpoint v offers up to b_v batteries; an edge needs at least w batteries carried. Starting at 1 with none, minimize batteries carried on arrival at n, or -1.
key_idea: Binary search a cap X: with batteries capped at X, propagate the maximum carry along the DAG in index order; feasible iff n is reachable.
solution:
1. Feasibility(X): best[1]=min(b_1,X); others -1 (unreachable).
2. Process vertices in increasing index (edges go s<t): for each edge s->t with best[s]>=w: best[t]=max(best[t], min(best[s]+b_t, X)).
3. Carrying more never hurts and the cap models taking fewer, so feasible iff best[n]>=0.
4. Binary search the smallest X in [0, 1e9]; if X=1e9 infeasible -> -1.
complexity: O((n+m) log W) time, O(n+m) space

X=1: best1=1, 1->2 ok best2=1, 2->3 ok best3=1 -> feasible.

brief: Process a_1..a_n from c=0, at each step either c+=a_i or c=|c+a_i|. Count choice sequences that reach the maximum possible final c, mod 998244353.
key_idea: The best play takes the absolute value once, at a position where the prefix sum is minimal; count choices that don't matter (when prefix >= 0) around each such position.
solution:
1. P_i = prefix sums, mn = min P_i.
2. If mn >= 0: every choice gives the same result -> 2^n.
3. Else for each i with P_i == mn: abs at i is essential; for j<i, abs is harmless only where P_j >= 0 (cnt of such j); after i the value stays >= 0 so all n-i choices are free.
4. Answer = sum over such i of 2^(cnt_{<i} + n - i) mod p.

brief: Given a number with up to 1e5 digits, sum (mod 1e9+7) all values obtained by deleting one non-empty contiguous substring of digits (leading zeros allowed; deleting all gives 0).
key_idea: Sum contributions per digit: deletion left of it keeps its place value; deletion right of it with q digits remaining gives place 10^q in q+1 ways.
solution:
1. Digit at index i (0-based), p = n-1-i digits to its right.
2. Deleted block entirely left of i: i(i+1)/2 ways, value d*10^p.
3. Deleted block entirely right: leaves q in [0,p-1] digits after it, q+1 ways each, value d*10^q -> d*S[p], S[p]=sum_{q<p}(q+1)10^q.
4. Answer = sum d_i*( i(i+1)/2 * 10^p + S[p] ) mod 1e9+7.

brief: n monsters in a row with health a_i. Choose a start and power x; the spell hits monsters expanding outward in an adversarial order, the k-th hit dealing x-(k-1). Minimize x that kills all monsters for the best start.
key_idea: For start i, monster j<i can be hit last at step n-j+1 and j>i at step j, so x >= a_j + (n-j) on the left and a_j + (j-1) on the right.
solution:
1. Use 1-indexed positions.
2. L[j]=a_j+n-j (worst case for a monster left of start), R[j]=a_j+j-1 (right of start).
3. pre[i]=max L[1..i-1], suf[i]=max R[i+1..n].
4. Answer = min over i of max(a_i, pre[i], suf[i]). Use long long.

Left: j=1 -> 4+4=8, j=2 -> 7. Right: j=4 -> 7, j=5 -> 8.
max(4,8,8)=8; other starts are no better -> 8 (matches).

brief: Weights of available masses 1..10 placed alternately on left/right pans; consecutive weights differ and after each placement the pan just used must be strictly heavier. Output a valid sequence of m weights or NO.
key_idea: State = (step, last weight, current lead d of the heavier pan, 1..10); next weight w must be != last and > d, giving new lead w-d. DFS with memo on failing states.
solution:
1. Lead after a placement: d = w - d_prev (>0 required), always in 1..10.
2. DFS(step, last, d): if step==m succeed; try each available w != last with w > d -> DFS(step+1, w, w-d).
3. Memoize failed states (1000*11*11) so each is explored once.
4. Start with DFS(0, 0, 0); print YES and the path, else NO.

Output YES 8 10 8 (matches).

brief: 2n jars (1=strawberry, 2=blueberry); Karlsson in the middle repeatedly empties the nearest full jar on the left or right. Minimize jars emptied so remaining full jars have equal counts of both types.
key_idea: Remaining jars = a prefix of the left half plus a suffix of the right half; need balance(prefix)+balance(suffix)=0; hash map of suffix balances to minimal removals.
solution:
1. Balance: +1 for type 1, -1 for type 2.
2. For the right half, for each suffix starting at j (n+1..2n+1), removed = j-(n+1); store in map best[balance] the minimal removed (iterate j from n+1 upward and keep the first).
3. For each prefix length i (0..n) of the left half, removed = n-i; look up best[-bal(prefix i)].
4. Answer = min over i of (n-i)+best[...]. Emptying everything always works (0=0).
complexity: O(n log n) with map (O(n) with an offset array)

Answer 2 (matches).

brief: Count strings with exact letter counts c_1..c_26 where equal letters are always an even distance apart, mod 998244353.
key_idea: Each letter lives entirely on odd or entirely on even positions; count subsets of (nonzero) letters filling exactly ceil(L/2) odd slots, times odd!*even!/prod c_i!.
solution:
1. L=sum c, O=ceil(L/2), E=floor(L/2).
2. Knapsack over letters with c_i>0: ways[s] = number of subsets with total s; need ways[O].
3. Arrangements for a fixed split = O!/prod_{odd letters} c_i! * E!/prod_{even letters} c_i! = O!*E!/prod_all c_i!, the same for every split.
4. Answer = ways[O] * O! * E! * inv(prod c_i!) mod p. Precompute factorials to 5e5.
complexity: O(26 * L) per test, O(maxL) precompute

Multinomial 2!*2!/(2!*1!*1!)=2.
Answer 2*2=4 (matches).

brief: On a huge strip, n traffic lights at p_i turn red at times l*k+d_i; each second you turn around if standing on a red light, then move one cell. For each start (facing right at time 0), decide if you eventually leave the strip.
key_idea: Only states (light index, time mod k, direction) matter; simulate jumps between consecutive lights and detect a repeated state (stuck forever) or running off past the last/first light (escape).
solution:
1. From start a, find the first light j with p_j >= a (binary search); none -> YES. Time t=(p_j-a) mod k, facing right.
2. At light i with time t: if t%k == d_i, flip direction.
3. Move to i+1 or i-1; if it doesn't exist -> YES. t += |p_next - p_i| (mod k).
4. Keep visited[(i, t, dir)]; revisiting -> NO (cycle).
5. States <= 2nk per query, fine for easy limits.

brief: n x m grid of heights; find the largest l such that some l x l square has every cell height >= l.
key_idea: Feasibility is monotone in l; check with a 2D prefix sum of cells with height >= l.
solution:
1. Binary search l in [1, n] (n<=m).
2. check(l): b[i][j]=(a[i][j]>=l); 2D prefix sums; any l x l window with sum l*l -> true.
3. Largest true l is the answer (l=1 always works since a>=1).
4. Store the grid flat (n*m<=1e6).

brief: n people queue for an escalator; each second the first person enters with probability p (otherwise everyone waits). Find the expected number of people on the escalator after t seconds.
key_idea: dp[i][k] = probability that exactly k people are on after i seconds.
solution:
1. dp[0][0]=1.
2. For k<n: dp[i+1][k+1] += dp[i][k]*p; dp[i+1][k] += dp[i][k]*(1-p).
3. k==n: dp[i+1][n] += dp[i][n] (queue empty).
4. Answer = sum k*dp[t][k]; print with enough precision (rolling 1D array is enough).

brief: n x n grid of heights; adding 1 to a whole row i costs a_i, to a whole column j costs b_j (each at most once). Minimize cost so no two side-adjacent cells are equal, or -1.
key_idea: Horizontal neighbors depend only on column choices, vertical only on row choices; solve two independent 0/1 chain DPs.
solution:
1. Rows: x_i in {0,1}. Rows i and i+1 conflict for delta=x_{i+1}-x_i iff some column j has h[i][j]-h[i+1][j]==delta (check delta in {-1,0,1}).
2. dp[i][x] = min cost for rows 1..i with row i choice x: dp[i][x]=x*a_i + min over valid y of dp[i-1][y].
3. Same for columns with b and horizontal pairs.
4. If either chain is impossible -> -1, else sum of the two minima. Use long long.

Columns: diffs within rows -1 and 1 -> delta 0 OK -> cost 0.
Answer 0 (matches).

brief: Binary string s (random in real tests); choose two substrings, read them as binary numbers, and maximize their bitwise OR; print it in binary.
key_idea: One substring is s from its first '1' to the end; the other is the same string shifted right by k, where k ranges only up to the position of the first '0' (expected tiny on random data).
solution:
1. Strip leading zeros: t = s from the first '1'; if no '1' print 0.
2. z = index of the first '0' in t; if none, print t.
3. For each shift k=1..z: candidate[i] = t[i] OR (i>=k ? t[i-k] : 0); keep the lexicographically largest (same length).
4. Shift k fills the first zero with a 1 from the run of leading ones; random data keeps z small so O(n*z).
complexity: O(n * z) time (z ~ small on random input), O(n) space

brief: Trampolines with strengths S_i; landing on i sends you to i+S_i and decreases S_i by 1 (min 1). Each pass starts anywhere and ends when you leave. Minimize passes to make all strengths 1.
key_idea: Go left to right: visits already arriving at i (cnt[i]) are free; start max(0,S_i-1-cnt[i]) new passes; the jumps from i land on i+2..i+S_i once each, surplus visits spill to i+1.
solution:
1. cnt[i] = number of times earlier passes land on i.
2. need = max(0, S_i-1-cnt[i]); ans += need; total visits v = cnt[i]+need.
3. While strength > 1, the jumps go to i+S_i, i+S_i-1, ..., i+2: add 1 to cnt[j] for j in [i+2, min(n, i+S_i)].
4. The remaining v-(S_i-1) visits (strength 1) go to i+1: cnt[i+1] += v-(S_i-1).
5. Direct loop is O(n^2) (n<=5000) or use a difference array.

brief: String s over the first k letters; for each query t, find the minimum number of letters to append to t so that it is no longer a subsequence of s (0 if it already isn't).
key_idea: Next-occurrence table nxt[i][c] plus dp[i] = 1 + min over c of dp[nxt[i][c]+1] (0 if c doesn't occur from i).
solution:
1. nxt[i][c] = smallest j>=i with s[j]==c, or n if none; build right to left.
2. dp[n]=1 (any letter fails); dp[i] = 1 + min over c of (nxt[i][c]==n ? 0 : dp[nxt[i][c]+1]).
3. Query: greedily match t using nxt; if it fails print 0; else at position p after the last matched char, print dp[p].
4. Memory: (n+1)*k ints (~104MB, limit 512MB).

brief: n seven-segment digits with some segments lit; turn on exactly k more segments (only unlit ones) so every digit is valid, maximizing the resulting number; else -1.
key_idea: Suffix feasibility DP can[i][j] (digits i..n-1 can use exactly j segments), then greedily pick the largest digit at each position that keeps the rest feasible.
solution:
1. cost[i][d] = #segments to add to make digit i show d, or -1 if a lit segment isn't in d's mask.
2. can[n][0]=true; can[i][j] = OR over d with cost c>=0 and c<=j of can[i+1][j-c].
3. If !can[0][k] -> -1.
4. For i=0..n-1: for d=9..0: if c=cost[i][d] valid and can[i+1][k-c]: output d, k-=c, break.
complexity: O(n * k * 10) time, O(n*k) bits space

brief: n monsters in order with powers a_i; m heroes (power p, endurance s) usable any number of times, one per day, each day killing consecutive monsters while power suffices up to s kills. Minimize days or -1.
key_idea: best[len] = max power among heroes with endurance >= len (suffix max); each day greedily extend while max monster so far <= best[len].
solution:
1. best[s]=max p over heroes with endurance exactly s; then suffix max so best[len] covers endurance >= len.
2. If max(a) > best[1] -> -1.
3. Each day from position i: len=0, mx=0; while i+len<n and max(mx,a[i+len]) <= best[len+1]: extend.
4. days++, i += len. Total work O(n) since each monster is consumed once.

Day1: 2,3 (len2, max3<=3). Day2: 11 (len2 would need 14<=3 no). Day3: 14. Day4: 1 then 8? max 8 > best[2]=3 -> just 1. Day5: 8.

brief: Count black/white colorings of a 2 x n grid with exactly k same-color connected components, mod 998244353.
key_idea: dp[i][k][pattern] over the 4 column patterns; the number of new components depends only on the previous and current pattern.
solution:
1. Patterns: 0=WW, 1=WB, 2=BW, 3=BB.
2. Init column 1: mono patterns 1 component, mixed patterns 2.
3. add(p,q): p mono: q==p ->0, q other mono ->1, q mixed ->1. p mixed: q mono ->0, q==p ->0, q opposite mixed ->2.
4. dp[i][j+add][q] += dp[i-1][j][p].
5. Answer = sum over patterns of dp[n][k].
complexity: O(n * k * 16) time, O(k) space with rolling arrays

Sample 2: n=4, k=1: only all-white or all-black -> 2 (matches).

brief: Tree with all edges of length k, rooted at 1. Moving the root to a neighbor costs c. Profit = (max distance from root) - (total move cost). Maximize profit.
key_idea: Moving the root to v costs c*depth(v) and gives k*ecc(v); eccentricity = max distance to the two diameter endpoints.
solution:
1. BFS from 1: depth[v]; farthest vertex A.
2. BFS from A: dA; farthest B; BFS from B: dB.
3. ecc(v) = max(dA[v], dB[v]) (in edges).
4. Answer = max over v of k*ecc(v) - c*depth(v). Use long long.
dry_run:
Sample 1: n=3, k=2, c=3, star center 1.
Root 1: ecc 1 -> 2*1 - 0 = 2.
Root 2: ecc 2 -> 4 - 3 = 1.
Answer 2 (matches).

brief: Ratings a_1..a_n; skip a non-empty contiguous block of contests. Starting from 0, each played contest moves the rating 1 toward a_i (+1 if below, -1 if above). Maximize the final rating.
key_idea: Three states: before the skip, inside the skip, after the skip; since the update is monotone in the current rating, keep the maximum per state.
solution:
1. upd(x,a) = x<a ? x+1 : (x>a ? x-1 : x), which is non-decreasing in x.
2. f0 = rating with no skip yet; f1 = best rating while inside the skip; f2 = best after the skip.
3. Per i: f2 = upd(max(f2, f1), a_i) (if valid); f1 = max(f1, f0) (skip i); f0 = upd(f0, a_i). Update in that order using previous values.
4. Answer = max(f1, f2) at the end (skip must be non-empty).

f0 after 1,2: 1,2. Skip contests 3..5 (f1=2).
Then 3: 2->3, 4: 3->4. f2=4.
Answer 4 (matches).

brief: Count black/white colorings of an n x m grid where every cell has at most one same-colored side neighbor, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Valid grids are either row-alternating stripes or column-alternating stripes; count = g(n)+g(m)-2 with Fibonacci-like g.
solution:
1. g(k) = number of valid 1 x k strips: g(1)=2, g(2)=4, g(k)=g(k-1)+g(k-2) (no three equal in a row).
2. If some row has two equal adjacent cells, every row is determined (each row is the complement of the previous) -> driven by the first column pattern: g(n) options; otherwise every row alternates and the first column decides: g(m) options.
3. The two chessboard colorings are counted in both families -> subtract 2.
4. Answer (g(n)+g(m)-2) mod p.

brief: n x n binary matrix; an operation at (i,j) flips every (x,y) with x>=i and x-i >= |y-j| (a downward cone). Find the minimum operations to make all zeros.
key_idea: Process cells top-down, left-right: a cell must be operated on iff its current value (after earlier cones) is 1; track cone coverage parity with three propagated arrays (straight, left edge, right edge).
solution:
1. A cell is only affected by operations at or above it, so greedy row by row is forced and optimal.
2. Row i interval of a cone = previous interval widened by 1 on each side. Keep parity arrays: cov (covered cells), L (left edges), R (right edges).
3. covPrev(i,j) = cov[i-1][j] ^ L[i-1][j+1] ^ R[i-1][j-1] (new cells from widened edges).
4. op = a[i][j] ^ covPrev; ans += op; cov[i][j]=covPrev^op; L[i][j]=L[i-1][j+1]^op; R[i][j]=R[i-1][j-1]^op.
5. Edges that leave the grid never return, so dropping them is safe. Use two rolling rows.

Row2 covPrev: cols 2..4 = 1, matching 01110 -> no ops.
Row3 cols 1..5 covered, matching 11111; rows 4,5 likewise -> ans=1 (matches).

brief: Tree, pieces P_A at a (paints white->red) and P_B at b (paints red->blue); each step A moves then B moves. Find the minimum steps to make all vertices blue.
key_idea: B should first meet A's red trail at the midpoint c of path a-b (after ceil(d/2) steps), then do a DFS tour from c: 2(n-1) - (max depth from c).
solution:
1. BFS from a to get parent pointers toward a and d=dist(a,b).
2. t = ceil(d/2) = (d+1)/2; walk t steps from b toward a to get c (vertex B reaches first that is already red).
3. From c, B must visit every vertex; a full tour returning is 2(n-1) steps, ending at the deepest vertex saves maxDist(c).
4. Answer = t + 2(n-1) - maxDist(c) (BFS from c). A always stays ahead painting red.
5. a==b: t=0, c=a.

t=1, c=1 (one step from 2 toward 1).
maxDist(1)=1 -> 1 + 2*1 - 1 = 2 (matches).

brief: Array of length m (up to 1e9) of zeros and n segments; choose a subset, each adds 1 on its range. Maximize max(a)-min(a).
key_idea: Make the minimum sit at position 1 or m: use only segments avoiding position 1 (or avoiding m) and take the maximum point coverage among them.
solution:
1. If the max is at x, take every segment containing x that avoids the chosen min position; the min ends at 1 or m (WLOG the endpoint on the far side).
2. Case A: segments with l>1; Case B: segments with r<m.
3. For each case, max overlap via sweep: events (l,+1), (r+1,-1), sort, prefix sum max.
4. Answer = max of the two cases (0 if no segments qualify).

Answer 1 (matches).

brief: Rearrange the digits of a (up to 1e18) to get the largest number not exceeding b, without leading zeros; an answer is guaranteed.
key_idea: If a is shorter than b, sort digits descending; otherwise fix digits left to right choosing the largest digit that still allows the smallest completion to stay <= b.
solution:
1. If len(a)<len(b): print digits of a sorted descending.
2. Else (equal lengths): res=""; available multiset of digits.
3. For each position, try digits d from 9 down to 0 (available): candidate = res + d + (remaining digits sorted ascending); if candidate <= b (string compare, same length) accept d.
4. Leading zero can't win because a valid answer exists and larger digits are tried first.

brief: Concatenate all permutations of 1..n in lexicographic order; count length-n windows whose sum is n(n+1)/2, mod 998244353.
key_idea: Answer = n*n! - sum_{j=1}^{n-1} n!/j!: a boundary-straddling window fails exactly when the left permutation's tail of length j is decreasing (n!/j! such permutations).
solution:
1. The n! windows aligned with a permutation are all good.
2. A window with the last n-k elements of P and the first k of the next permutation Q is good iff Q keeps P's first k elements, i.e. P's tail of length j=n-k is NOT decreasing.
3. Permutations with a decreasing tail of length j: n!/j!; so good windows for that split = n! - n!/j! (the last permutation, always decreasing, has no successor and cancels out).
4. Total = n! + sum_{j=1}^{n-1} (n! - n!/j!) = n*n! - sum_{j=1}^{n-1} n!/j!, computing n!/j! = (j+1)...n iteratively, mod p.

brief: Grid of '.'/'X'; a cell is exitable if you can leave the grid moving only up/left through empty cells. For queries of column ranges [x1,x2], decide if the exitability pattern of that subgrid uniquely determines the grid.
key_idea: Ambiguity arises exactly when some cell has 'X' above it and 'X' to its left; mark column j bad if g[i-1][j]=='X' and g[i][j-1]=='X', then a query is NO iff a bad column lies in (x1, x2].
solution:
1. For each column j>=2 (1-indexed), bad[j]=1 if some row i>=2 has g[i-1][j]=='X' and g[i][j-1]=='X'.
2. Such a cell is non-exitable whether empty or filled -> undeterminable, and only if both blockers are inside the range (columns j-1 and j).
3. Prefix sums P over bad.
4. Query: YES iff P[x2]-P[x1]==0 (column x1 itself has its left neighbor outside the range).

Query (4,5): bad column 5 in (4,5] -> NO.
Query (5,5): (5,5] empty -> YES; (1,3) -> YES (matches).

brief: Directed graph (n<=100) and a walk p_1..p_m; find the shortest subsequence (keeping first and last) such that p is a shortest path visiting those vertices in order.
key_idea: Floyd-Warshall distances; greedily skip vertices while the walk segment from the last kept vertex is still a shortest path.
solution:
1. Floyd-Warshall on the adjacency matrix (unit weights).
2. Keep p_1; last = 1.
3. For i=2..m: if dist[p_last][p_i] < i-last, the segment is no longer shortest -> keep p_{i-1}, last=i-1.
4. Keep p_m. Output the kept list.

brief: n players with distinct strengths on two maps; battles on any map eliminate the weaker. For each player, can they be the last one standing?
key_idea: Winners form a suffix in order of map-1 strength; extend the suffix down while someone outside has higher map-2 strength than someone inside.
solution:
1. Sort players by a ascending.
2. pm[i] = max b over sorted[0..i], sm[i] = min b over sorted[i..n-1].
3. Find the largest k such that k==0 or pm[k-1] < sm[k] (nobody below can beat anyone in the suffix on either map).
4. Players at sorted positions >= k print 1, others 0 (the top-a player can always be reached through the chain).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Problems 1..n with scores a_i and parameters b_i; you start at problem 1. Submitting i moves to the largest unseen j<i; skipping i moves to the largest unseen j<=b_i. Maximize total submitted score.
key_idea: If you end with max reached index i, you can submit everything in 1..i except what you skipped; minimize skipped cost to reach i with Dijkstra on edges i->i-1 (0) and i->b_i (a_i).
solution:
1. Graph: edge i -> i-1 with cost 0 (move back), edge i -> b_i with cost a_i (skip i).
2. Dijkstra from 1: dist[i] = min total score of skipped problems to reach i.
3. Reaching i means all problems 1..i are eventually given and solvable except skipped ones.
4. Answer = max over i of prefix(a_1..a_i) - dist[i]. Use long long.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
